story: by griffin kelly staff writer lake placid a court case related to
title: By GRIFFIN KELLY Staff Writer 	LAKE PLACID — A court case related to the death of Saige Borden on Lake Placid was recently dismissed from village court. 	In December 2017, Camilla Varoli was charged with three misdemeanor counts of unlawfully dealing with a child for allegedly providing alcohol to minors while at her parents' property, Camp Gordon. However, the case was dismissed Nov. 12, when it was discovered that the alleged crime actually took place in the town of North Elba. 	Village and town Justice Dean Dietrich said, "I currently have no charges pending in North Elba, but that could change." 	"It was a clerical error, and I just wonder how can that have happened," Borden's mother Suzanne said Sunday. "I think (Varoli) should be tried again in the right jurisdiction. There's no reason why it shouldn't be picked up by the town." 	Borden's father Rob also believes the investigation into his daughter's death has been mishandled and prolonged since the beginning. 	"It's taken too much time and it's very frustrating," he said. 	The statute of limitations on misdemeanors in New York typically lasts between one to two years, and it's getting close to the two-year mark since Varoli was originally charged. 	In the early hours of May 12, 2017, Borden, 20, drowned after the canoe she was in tipped, sending her and two friends, Varoli and Jonni Springer, into the cold waters of Lake Placid. Varoli and Springer made it to shore, but Borden didn't. There were no life jackets on board, and the three had been drinking and taking recreational drugs in the hours leading up to the incident, according to an autopsy report from the Franklin County Coroner's office and Adirondack Health, which cited police reports. 	When Borden arrived at the Adirondack Medical Center in Saranac Lake, her temperature was 80.6 degrees Fahrenheit, 18 degrees lower than the average body temperature. After four hours and Borden going in and out of normal cardiac rhythm, resuscitation was terminated and she was pronounced dead. 	Seven months later, state police charged Varoli with unlawfully dealing with a child and petit larceny for allegedly purchasing alcohol with a stolen credit card belonging to Borden's mother Suzanne. Matthew Pilawa was charged with criminal nuisance in the second degree for allowing underage consumption of alcohol and drug use to take place at his home in the Lake Placid the night before Borden drowned. In September 2018, six jurors in town court found Varoli not guilty of petit larceny. | News, Sports, Jobs

title: Karla Peterson: After the 'Laurel Canyon' documentary series, check out these vital music scenes (EDITORS: Corrects "Gladys Knight" with "Martha Reeves" in graf 6.) (PHOTO) By Karla Peterson The San Diego Union-Tribune (TNS) For me, watching the Epix network's "Laurel Canyon" was the perfect weekend diversion. In addition to being a window into a time of life-changing music (Joni Mitchell, sigh), the two-part documentary on the Southern California singer-songwriter scene was also a window that looked out on somewhere other than my front yard. I really needed that window. As a music fan who won't be going to a concert anytime soon, nothing makes me happier than a deep dive into a music scene. Hearing new stories about the songs I love and discovering new objects of musical obsession are my idea of a great escape. If your happy place also features a mixing board, grainy concert footage from grimy clubs and/or guest appearances by men in dresses, here are some magical mystery tours that are ready to take you away. —"Hitsville: The Making of Motown" Was there was ever a better, more influential musical movement than the one that exploded out of the Detroit-based Motown Records? One look at the label's mind-blowing lineup — Marvin Gaye! Smokey Robinson! Stevie Wonder! Diana Ross and the Supremes! The Jackson 5! — and the correct answer would be, "Why are you even asking?" Produced by Showtime in honor of the label's 60th anniversary, 2019's "Hitsville: The Making of Motown" is a big pop culture scrapbook featuring interviews with most of the key players (founder Berry Gordy Jr., Smokey Robinson, Martha Reeves, the unstoppable songwriting and producing team of Lamont Dozier and Brian and Eddie Holland); a bonanza of performance clips; and a glorious wealth of treasures from the Motown vaults. Thanks to the cooperation of Gordy, who is one of the documentary's executive producers, filmmakers Gabe and Benjamin Turner had access to many one-of-a-kind goodies. The gems include the audio recordings from the company's famous quality-control meetings, where everyone in the Motown family was invited to weigh in on the commercial prospects of the newest batch of singles. The boss was not always right. At less than two hours long, "Hitsville: The Making of Motown" is too short to truly do justice to all of the label's deserving artists, its many hits or its impact on music and history. And with Gordy so prominently on board, the company is shown in a consistently flattering light, making the film short on shadows and nuance. In the end, "Hitsville" will definitely leave you wanting to hear more and learn more, which is not a bad thing. As Gordy himself says: "The sky is not the limit. The sky is the first stop." (Streaming and DVD) —"Love Goes to Buildings on Fire" by Will Hermes The full title of Will Hermes' indispensable 2011 book is "Love Goes to Buildings on Fire: Five Years in New York That Changed Music Forever." It's long, but it's not wrong. Hermes' book covers the wildly erratic years of 1973 to 1977, when New York City was both a crime-ridden, rat-infested hellhole and a hotbed of creativity. During these five crazy years, the Big (Rotten) Apple's dive bars, underground dance clubs and cheap artists' lofts were home to the groundbreaking musicians and tastemakers who brought us the sounds of punk rock, hip-hop, disco, post-Coltrane jazz and more. With the help of a colorful cast of characters — the cross-dressing New York Dolls, Grandmaster Flash, Studio 54 DJ Nicky Siano, CBGB founder Hilly Kristal, Bruce Springsteen — Hermes paints a kaleidoscopic portrait of a place where artistic explosions were going off every few seconds. And in the process of rocking New York, these movers, shakers and scene-makers kicked off pop culture movements that rocked the world. Hermes' "Love Goes to Buildings on Fire" (named after a Talking Heads song) is an exhaustive, exhilarating look at how a dark time in a godforsaken place produced music that still makes you want to dance, sweat and scream until you drop. Save some energy for reading the discography, which should keep your ears ringing until 2073. —"Hip-Hop Evolution" Over four smart, dynamic seasons, this Netflix series explores hip-hop in all its dizzying permutations, with each four-episode season digging into pivotal moments in the hip-hop story. Leave it to a Canadian series to give us the practical guide to hip-hop we always needed. Season 1 of "Hip-Hop Evolution" gives us the history portion, with episodes dedicated to the genre's New York roots, the essential Run-DMC and gangsta rap. Season 2 is the geography tutorial, with chapters on Southern hip-hop and jazz- and Latin-influenced groups. Season 3 looks at grudge matches, deaths and the out-there styling of OutKast and alternative hip-hop. And Season 4 brings us the sticky, rootsy sounds of Atlanta and Memphis; the visions of Missy Elliott and Timbaland; and the game-changing power of mixtapes. The episodes usually run under 40 minutes, but they are packed with high-profile interviews, juicy anecdotes, and enough videos to turn an afternoon of streaming into one heck of an all-nighter. (Netflix) —Ken Burns' "Country Music" While it only seems like the prolific Burns puts out a new massive documentary series every month or so, it is still possible that you missed his encyclopedic look at country music when the series was originally released last fall. No time like the present to catch up! Over eight two-hour episodes, "Country Music" looks at the history of a genre that was rooted in slave songs and Appalachian "hillbilly" tunes, but went on to weave in big-band swing, juke-joint twang, Bob Dylan's folk poetry and Garth Brooks' arena-rock polish. Yes, it's the Grand Ole Opry and "Hee Haw." It is also so much more. A big tent deserves a big show, and "Country Music" takes time to explore the SoCal stylings of the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band; Dolly Parton's singular career; Johnny Cash's rise, drug-fueled fall and rebirth; and the challenges facing black performers like Charley Pride and Darius Rucker. You might think you aren't a country fan, but the staggering collection of voices and stories featured in "Country Music" will certainly prove you wrong. Any music community that has room for Minnie Pearl and Merle Haggard has room for you. (DVD and streaming)
